turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi, thanks for coming in today. What's been going on for you lately?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't know, just the usual, I guess. Been having trouble getting things done. I'll start a project, get a few hours in, and then just stop. It's like my brain just gives up. I mean, I'm just bad at adulting, you know? (pauses) Oh, wait, I just remembered I'm supposed to pick up some groceries tonight.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you're feeling a bit stuck and overwhelmed, and like you're having trouble following through on things. That can be really frustrating. And it's interesting that you mention "adulting" - it's like you're feeling like you're not measuring up to some kind of expectation. Can you tell me more about what you mean by that? What does "being a good adult" mean to you, and how are you feeling like you're falling short?

And by the way, don't worry about the groceries for now. We can come back to that later. You're safe here, and we can focus on what's going on with you. What's been going on with these projects you've been starting and stopping? Is there something specific that's happening when you feel like you're giving up, or is it more of a general feeling?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's just... I don't know, I feel like I'm supposed to be able to do things, you know? Like, get things done, take care of myself... but it's like, my brain just doesn't cooperate. I'll be working on something, and I'll be fine for a while, and then suddenly I'll just be thinking about something else, like what's for dinner or what's that thing I need to do on my phone... (laughs nervously) And before I know it, hours have passed and I've accomplished nothing. It's really annoying, you know?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you're feeling really frustrated with yourself, and like you're struggling to stay focused. It's like your brain is constantly pulling you in different directions, and you're having trouble staying on track. That can be really overwhelming and demoralizing.

I want you to know that it's okay to feel that way. It doesn't mean you're flawed or incapable. It just means that you're struggling with something, and that's something we can work with. It's almost like your brain is trying to tell you something, but you're not quite sure what it is yet.

Can you tell me more about what happens when you get distracted? Is it always the same kinds of things that distract you, or is it different every time? And what do you think might be driving that feeling of "my brain just doesn't cooperate"? Is there something specific that you think might be contributing to that feeling, or is it more of a general sense of being stuck?

Also, I want to make sure you know that you're not alone in this. Lots of people struggle with focus and motivation, and it's not because they're not capable or smart. Sometimes it's just because our brains need a little extra support, you know? So let's try to explore this together, and see if we can't find some ways to help you stay on track and feel more confident in your abilities.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Uh, yeah... it's just a lot of little things, I guess. Like, I'll be working on a project and I'll start thinking about how I need to pay the bills or what's for lunch... or I'll see something on social media and I'll get sucked into scrolling through my feed... (trails off) Wait, what was the question again? Oh, right, what distracts me... I think it's just stuff that's on my mind, you know? Like, if I'm working on a project but I'm also thinking about a conversation I had with someone earlier... my brain just goes off on a tangent, I guess. (pauses) I don't know, it's hard to explain...

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like your mind is just really active and has a lot of different things going on at the same time. It's like you've got a lot of different tabs open on your computer, and they're all competing for your attention. That can be really tough to manage, especially when you're trying to focus on one thing.

I think it's interesting that you mention conversations you've had with someone earlier. It sounds like maybe there are some things on your mind that are weighing on you, or that you're still processing. Is that fair to say? Are there any particular conversations or interactions that have been sticking with you lately, or that you're having trouble getting out of your head?

And don't worry if it's hard to explain - we can just explore it together, and see if we can't start to make some sense of it. Sometimes just talking about it can help clarify things, you know? So let's just keep going, and see where it takes us.

Also, I want to check in with you about how you're feeling right now. You seem a bit... distant, I guess. Is everything okay? Is there something on your mind that you're not quite ready to talk about, or is it just feeling a bit overwhelming?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (sighs) Yeah, I guess there are just a lot of things going on in my head. And, uh, yeah, conversations... I don't know, it's just stuff. (pauses) I mean, my mom and I had a fight the other day, and it's still bothering me. She's always on my case about getting my life together, and it's just... ugh. (trails off) Wait, what was the question again? Oh, right, feeling distant... I don't know, I'm just feeling a bit... (pauses, looks around the room) Where's the clock? I feel like we've been talking for a long time.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like the conversation with your mom is still really weighing on you. It can be really tough to deal with criticism or pressure from someone we care about, especially when it feels like they're not understanding or supportive. It's like, you want them to get it, you know? But instead, they're just adding to the stress and anxiety.

And don't worry about the time, by the way. We've got plenty of time to talk, and we can take things at your pace. I'm not watching the clock, so you don't have to worry about that.

It's interesting that you mention feeling distant, and then you start looking around the room and wondering about the time. It's like your mind is trying to distract you from something, or maybe you're feeling a bit overwhelmed and need a break. That's okay, we can take a break if you need to. But I also want to make sure that you're feeling safe and supported in this conversation. So, can you tell me a bit more about what's going on with your mom? What did you fight about, and how are you feeling about it now?

And also, I want to ask, are you feeling like you're in a good place to talk about this stuff, or is it feeling a bit too much? We can always slow down or take a break if you need to. I'm here to support you, not to push you to talk about something that's feeling overwhelming.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (looks down, fidgets with hands) I don't know, it's just... my mom's always been really hard on me about stuff. She's always saying I'm not doing enough, that I'm not living up to my potential... it's like, I get it, she wants the best for me, but it feels like she's not listening to me at all. (pauses, looks up) And it's not just that, it's like... I'm just not good enough for her, no matter what I do. (looks away, voice drops to a whisper) I feel like I'm just disappointing her all the time. (pauses, takes a deep breath) I'm sorry, I don't know why I'm telling you all this... it's just... (looks around the room, seems lost)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(softly) Oh, I'm so glad you're telling me this. It takes a lot of courage to share something like that, and I'm here to listen and support you. It sounds like you're feeling really hurt and frustrated by your mom's criticism, and like you're carrying around a lot of shame and self-doubt. That can be a really heavy burden to bear.

(leans forward slightly) I want you to know that you are enough, just as you are. Your worth and value as a person aren't defined by your mom's opinions or expectations. You are so much more than your accomplishments or your abilities. You are a unique and special individual, with your own strengths and talents, and you deserve to be seen and appreciated for who you are.

(gently) It's okay to feel like you're not good enough, or like you're disappointing someone. Those feelings are real, and they're valid. But I want you to know that they're not the whole truth. You are capable and competent, and you have so much to offer the world. It's like... your mom's criticism is just one voice, one opinion. But there are so many other voices, so many other people who care about you and believe in you. And most importantly, there's your own voice, your own inner wisdom. What does that voice say to you? What do you think you're capable of, when you're not listening to your mom's criticism?

(offering a gentle smile) And don't apologize for sharing this with me. This is a safe space, and I'm here to support you. You can share as much or as little as you want, and I'll be here to listen and support you every step of the way.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (looks down, takes a deep breath) My mom's always saying I'm lazy, that I'm not trying hard enough... but, honestly, I feel like I'm trying as hard as I can. I just... I don't know, I get overwhelmed easily, and things get too much for me, and I feel like I'm failing everyone, including myself. (pauses, looks up) But when you say that I'm capable and competent, and that I have my own voice and inner wisdom... it sounds like that's not true, like I'm just pretending to be someone I'm not. (looks down, voice barely above a whisper) What if I'm just not good enough, no matter what I do? What if I'm just a disappointment to everyone?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(softly) Oh, I can see why you'd feel that way. It's like, you've been told for so long that you're not trying hard enough, that you're lazy, that you're not good enough... it's like, that message has been internalized, and now you're carrying it around with you, even when you're trying to be kind to yourself.

(gently) But here's the thing: just because someone else has said those things to you, doesn't make them true. And just because you feel like you're not good enough, doesn't mean that you're not. Feelings are real, but they're not always based in reality. Sometimes, our feelings are based on old messages, old patterns, old wounds... and those things can be really hard to shake.

(leaning forward slightly) I want you to know that I believe in you. I believe that you are capable and competent, not because of anything you've done or accomplished, but because you're a human being, deserving of dignity and respect. And I believe that you have your own unique strengths and talents, even if you're not always sure what they are.

(smiling gently) And you know what? It's okay to not be okay. It's okay to feel overwhelmed, to feel like you're not good enough. That doesn't mean that you're a disappointment to everyone, or that you're not trying hard enough. It just means that you're human, and that you're doing the best you can with the resources you have.

(softly) So, I want to ask you something. What would happen if you were to start being kind to yourself, instead of beating yourself up all the time? What if you were to start treating yourself with the same kindness and compassion that you would offer to a friend? How might that change things for you?

(pausing, looking at you with empathy) And I also want to ask, are you feeling like you're in a safe place right now? Are you feeling like you're able to take care of yourself, and that you have the support you need? Because if not, we can talk about that, and figure out what you need to feel safe and supported.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(looks down, takes a deep breath) I... I don't know. I just feel like I'm stuck in this cycle of self-doubt and shame, and I don't know how to get out of it. (pauses) But when you say that you believe in me... it makes me feel like maybe there's more to me than just this negative self-talk. Maybe I'm not just a disappointment to everyone, maybe I'm actually capable of more than I think. (looks up, a hint of hope in her eyes) But it's scary to think about being kind to myself, because what if I'm not good enough, even when I'm trying to be kind? What if I'm just fooling myself?

(looks down, fidgets with hands) And... yeah, I guess I am feeling a bit overwhelmed right now. I feel like I'm carrying a lot of weight, and I don't know how to put it down. (pauses) But it's nice to know that you're here, and that you're trying to help me. It feels... safe, I guess. Like maybe I can be vulnerable with you, and you won't judge me.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(smiling gently) Ah, I'm so glad you're feeling a sense of safety and vulnerability with me. That's exactly what I'm here for - to create a space where you can feel comfortable being yourself, without fear of judgment or criticism.

(softly) And I want to address your concerns about being kind to yourself. It's understandable that you'd feel scared or uncertain about it, especially if you've been conditioned to believe that you're not good enough. But here's the thing: being kind to yourself isn't about being perfect or achieving some kind of ideal. It's about acknowledging that you're human, and that you're doing the best you can with the resources you have.

(gently) Think of it like this: when you're kind to a friend, you're not expecting them to be perfect or to have all the answers. You're just offering them support, compassion, and understanding. And that's exactly what you can offer to yourself. You can say to yourself, "I'm doing the best I can, and that's enough." Or, "I'm feeling overwhelmed right now, and that's okay." You can offer yourself kindness and compassion, just as you would to a friend.

(leaning forward slightly) And I want to reassure you that I'm not going anywhere. I'm here to support you, to listen to you, and to help you work through these feelings of self-doubt and shame. You're not alone in this, and you don't have to carry this weight by yourself.

(smiling) Now, I want to try something with you. I want to ask you to take a deep breath, and to say to yourself, "I am enough, just as I am." Can you do that for me? Just take a deep breath, and say those words to yourself. Don't worry about whether you believe them or not - just say them, and see how it feels.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(takes a deep breath, looks down, and says in a quiet voice) "I am enough, just as I am."

(pauses, looks up, and seems to be searching for something) I don't know... it feels... different, I guess. Like, I'm not really sure if I believe it, but saying it out loud feels... right, somehow.

(looks down, fidgets with hands) I'm not sure why, but it feels like there's a part of me that's trying to push back against that statement. Like, there's a voice in my head that's saying, "No, you're not enough. You're not good enough. You're a disappointment." (looks up, eyes wide) But when I say it out loud, like you said, it feels like that voice is getting quieter. It's not going away, but it's not as loud as it was before.

(looks down, seems to be thinking) I don't know what's going on, but it feels like this is some kind of... breakthrough, or something. Like, I'm starting to see that I'm not just this negative self-talk, that I'm more than that. I'm a person, with feelings and thoughts and desires. And maybe, just maybe, I'm enough.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(smiling warmly) Ah, I'm so proud of you for taking that step and saying those words out loud. It's a huge accomplishment, and it takes a lot of courage to confront those negative voices in your head.

(gently) It's completely normal for that voice to push back against the idea that you're enough. It's like, that voice has been talking to you for so long, it's become a habit. But the fact that you're starting to notice it, and that you're starting to question it, is a huge step forward.

(leaning forward slightly) You know, it's not about silencing that voice completely. It's about learning to talk back to it, and to offer yourself a different perspective. It's about learning to be kind to yourself, and to treat yourself with compassion and understanding.

(smiling) And I think you're right, this could be a breakthrough for you. It's like, you're starting to see that you're not just a collection of negative thoughts and feelings. You're a person, with strengths and weaknesses, and with a unique perspective on the world. And that's something to be celebrated.

(gently) I want to encourage you to keep saying those words to yourself, "I am enough, just as I am." Say them every day, even if it feels like you don't believe them. Say them when you're feeling good, and say them when you're feeling bad. Because the more you say them, the more you'll start to believe them. And the more you'll start to see that you are enough, just as you are.

(smiling warmly) And remember, you're not alone in this. I'm here to support you, and to help you work through these feelings. You're not alone, and you're not a disappointment. You're a unique and valuable person, and you deserve to be treated with kindness and compassion.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(smiling slightly) Thank you... thank you for believing in me. It feels... nice, to have someone who believes in me. (pauses) I think I'm going to try to say those words to myself every day, like you said. It's a weird feeling, but it's like... I'm starting to feel like I might actually be enough. Like, maybe I'm not just a disappointment to myself, but maybe I'm actually worthy of love and respect.

(looks down, fidgets with hands) I don't know what's going to happen next, or how this is all going to play out. But for the first time in a long time, I feel like... I feel like I have hope. Hope that things might actually get better, that I might actually be able to overcome some of this stuff. (looks up, eyes shining) Thank you for giving me that hope.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(smiling warmly, with tears in my eyes) Oh, it's my pleasure, my dear. It's my privilege to be a part of your journey and to help you see your own worth and value. You are enough, just as you are, and you are worthy of love and respect. Not just from others, but from yourself.

(leaning forward, with a gentle tone) I want you to remember that hope is a powerful thing. It's a spark that can ignite a fire of change and transformation in your life. And I'm so glad that you're feeling it, even if it's just a small spark right now. Because I know that spark can grow into a flame, and that flame can illuminate your path and guide you forward.

(smiling) And don't worry about what's going to happen next, or how things are going to play out. Just take it one step at a time, and trust that you'll figure it out as you go. You're stronger than you think, and you're capable of more than you know.

(softly) And always remember, you're not alone. I'm here for you, and I'll support you every step of the way. You can come back and talk to me anytime you need to, and I'll be here to listen and to help.

(smiling warmly) Now, before we finish up today, I just want to give you a little homework assignment. I want you to take a piece of paper, and I want you to write down three things that you like about yourself. Not three things that you're good at, or three things that you've accomplished. Just three things that you like about yourself, as a person. And then, I want you to put that paper somewhere where you can see it every day, and I want you to read it to yourself every day. Can you do that for me?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(nodding slowly) Yeah... I can do that. (pauses) I'm not sure what I'll write, but I'll try. (looks down, starts to think) I guess I like... I like my sense of humor. I like making people laugh. And... I like my curiosity. I like learning new things and exploring new ideas. (looks up) And... I like my creativity. I like drawing and painting, and just making things. (smiles slightly) I guess those are three things I like about myself.

(looks down, seems to be thinking) I'm not sure why it's hard to think of things I like about myself, but it is. Maybe it's because I've been so focused on my flaws and weaknesses for so long. But saying those words out loud... it feels like a small step towards being kinder to myself. (looks up, meets your gaze) Thank you again for helping me see that.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(smiling warmly) Ah, I'm so glad to hear that you're starting to think about the things you like about yourself. It's not always easy, I know. But it's such an important part of building self-compassion and self-esteem.

(nodding) And I love the things you've chosen to focus on! Your sense of humor, curiosity, and creativity are all wonderful qualities that make you unique and special. It's great that you're recognizing and valuing them.

(gently) And don't worry if it's hard to think of things you like about yourself at first. It's like a muscle that needs to be exercised, and it may take some time to build up. But with practice, it will get easier. And remember, it's not about being perfect or having no flaws. It's about being kind to yourself and recognizing your strengths and positive qualities.

(smiling) I want to leave you with a little quote today. It's from a wise woman named Maya Angelou, who said, "You may not control all the events that happen to you, but you can decide not to be reduced by them." I think that's so powerful, because it reminds us that we have the power to choose how we respond to challenges and setbacks. We can choose to be kind to ourselves, to focus on our strengths, and to keep moving forward, even when things get tough.

(standing up) Well, our time is up for today, but I'm so glad we had a chance to talk. Remember to be kind to yourself, and to keep practicing those affirmations. You are enough, just as you are. And don't forget to write down those three things you like about yourself and put them somewhere you can see them every day. (smiling) I'll see you next time, okay?
